sections.title: Mental model — Big-O, Θ, Ω as promises

blocks.md: **O(f)**: *won't grow meaningfully faster than f* (upper promise). **Ω(f)**: *at least f on some inputs* (lower promise). **Θ(f)**: *exactly the f family* (tight). Interviews say "complexity?" and expect Θ-style answers with O vocabulary.

rows.label: "Bubble sort is Ω(n)"
rows.left: can't beat one pass (must inspect all) ✓

rows.label: "Counting inversions via mergesort is Θ(n log n)"
rows.left: tightly n log n in AND out

rows.label: "Quicksort is O(n²) but usually Θ(n log n)"
rows.left: worst-case ceiling differs from typical behavior

items: **Sequential blocks ADD**: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²) — the biggest term owns the total
**Nested loops MULTIPLY**, but inner bound may shrink (`j<i` triangle ≈ n²/2 → still Θ(n²))
**Recursion**: count tree nodes × per-node work. Halving depth + linear merge = T(n)=2T(n/2)+n ⇒ Θ(n log n)
**Amortized**: rare spikes averaged over a sequence (vector growth) — quote as amortized O(1)

items.explain: One subproblem, half size, constant work per level → levels = log n.

items.q: Triangle nested loop `for i<n: for j<i` performs…
items.explain: Half of n² still lives in the n² family.

items.q: Which claim about linear search is TRUE?
items.explain: Upper ceiling full scan; best case first element.

blocks.md: Memorize this table cold — interviewers probe whether you know what each container CHARGES:

segments.name: vector · random access O(1)
segments.desc: push_back amortized O(1) · insert/erase middle O(n) · sort member-free

segments.name: stack / queue
segments.desc: adapter over deque — all core ops O(1)

segments.name: priority_queue
segments.desc: push/pop Θ(log n) · top O(1) · NO decrease-key

segments.name: set/map (tree)
segments.desc: insert/erase/find Θ(log n) · ITERATED IN SORTED ORDER

segments.name: unordered_set/map (hash)
segments.desc: avg O(1), worst O(n) · iteration order unspecified

blocks.label: algorithms that ride on sorted order
blocks.code:
vector<int> v = {5, 2, 8, 2};
sort(v.begin(), v.end());                 // 2 2 5 8

bool exists = binary_search(v.begin(), v.end(), 5);   // true
auto lo = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);  // first >= 2 -> idx0
auto up = upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);  // first >  2 -> idx2
cout << up - lo;                          // COUNT of 2s = 2

// rotate, reverse, accumulate:
cout << accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);   // sum, ll accumulator!
cout << __builtin_popcount(13);                // bits: 3
blocks.py:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
v = sorted([5, 2, 8, 2])          # [2,2,5,8]

lo = bisect_left(v, 2)            # first >= 2 -> 0
up = bisect_right(v, 2)           # first > 2  -> 2
print(up - lo)                    # count of 2s = 2

print(sum(v))                     # accumulate
print(bin(13).count('1'))         # popcount equivalent

blocks.md: **unordered_map = array of buckets + hash(key) → bucket. Everything follows from collisions + load factor.**

items: **load factor = size ÷ buckets** — crossing max triggers REHASH: all elements re-bucketed, iterators die
average O(1) assumes decent hash spread; adversarial keys can pile into ONE bucket → O(n) per op
`operator[]` non-const & INSERTS missing keys — use `.find()` when absence is meaningful
custom key struct? You supply hash + equality (or specialize std::hash)

blocks.label: safe patterns
blocks.py:
from collections import defaultdict
m = defaultdict(int)
if 'key' in m:                    # lookup WITHOUT inserting
    use(m['key'])

m.reserve_equivalent = null       # no reserve; dict grows amortized
# max_load_factor tuning is internal - rely on CPython's adaptive sizing

sections.title: Problem set — L2 ladder (container choice + analysis)

items.title: Two Sum
items.statement: Indices of two numbers summing to target. Solve O(n) with unordered_map; explain the naive O(n²) you avoided.
hints: For each x ask map: seen target−x?
Insert AFTER checking to avoid self-pair.

items.title: Contains Duplicate
items.statement: Any value twice? Then discuss why sort+scan also passes and compare costs.
hints: Set insert returns pair<it,bool>.
Sort route: adjacent equals after Θ(n log n).

items.title: Valid Anagram
items.statement: Same letters same counts? Use 26-array; then say when you'd switch to unordered_map.
hints: Increment for s, decrement for t, check zeros.
Unicode/arbitrary chars → hash map instead.

items.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
items.statement: Unique common elements — implement with unordered_set; state complexities of both build and probe phases.
hints: Set the smaller array; scan larger against it.
Result uniqueness: erase on match or second set.

items.title: Missing Number
items.statement: [0..n] with one missing. Sum-formula AND XOR solutions; watch overflow reasoning.
hints: Expected sum n(n+1)/2 minus actual — use long long.
XOR route: pairs cancel, survivor is answer.

items.title: Merge Sorted Array (in-place)
items.statement: nums1 has trailing space; merge nums2 without extra buffer.
hints: Fill from the BACK with three pointers.
Largest goes last — avoids overwriting unread data.

items.title: Kth Smallest in Array
items.statement: kth smallest via sort AND via heap; compare costs aloud (n log n vs n log k).
hints: Heap route: keep size-k MAX-heap, pop on overflow.
Answer sits at pq.top() at the end.

items.title: Next Greater Element
items.statement: First greater to the right for each element (circular-free version). Stack+map pipeline.
hints: Walk right-to-left; pop smaller tops.
Store answers in value→value map for query phase.

items.title: Sort by Length (comparator drill)
items.statement: Sort strings ascending by length; equal lengths keep original relative order — justify stable_sort vs sort here.
hints: Stability matters ONLY because tie-order must persist.
Lambda comparing sizes; strict `<` only.

items.title: Range Count Queries
items.statement: Sorted array, q queries [a,b]: how many elements inside? Must be O(log n) per query.
hints: upper_bound(b) − lower_bound(a).
Never rescan per query — that's O(nq).

revisionCard: ADD sequential, MULTIPLY nested; biggest term owns the total
Recurrence intuition: halving+linear work ⇒ Θ(n log n); halving+constant ⇒ Θ(log n)
vector push_back amortized O(1); middle insert O(n)
map/tree Θ(log n)+sorted iteration · unordered avg O(1)+rehash storms+no order
priority_queue: push/pop log n, top O(1), NO decrease-key
operator[] inserts silently — find() when absence matters
Comparator must be strict (<) — never <= inside sort

glossary.def: Upper ceiling / tight bound / floor on growth family.
Sequence-average cost after spreading rare expensive operations.
Bucket-array regrowth re-placing every element; invalidates iterators.
First-not-less / first-greater positions in sorted ranges — bracket queries.
std::sort's hybrid (quick+heap+insertion) guaranteeing Θ(n log n) worst case.
Preserves original order of equal keys (stable_sort, merge-based).
Lowering a heap item's priority in place — std::priority_queue lacks it; design around it.
